title: The overflowing cup
hookLine: the master Nan-in pours tea for a professor until it spills: you are already full (Zen story, Japan)

cards: A university professor has come to call on a Zen master named Nan-in. The story sets it in Japan, in the Meiji era. The professor wants to learn about Zen, and he has a lot to say about it.
He's read the books. He has theories. He talks, and talks.
Nan-in says almost nothing. He makes tea, sets a cup in front of the professor, and begins to pour. The cup fills to the brim.
Nan-in keeps pouring. Tea runs over the rim, across the table, onto the floor.

teach.h: IT'S FULL! NOTHING MORE WILL GO IN!
teach.b: The professor can't stand it. Stop, he says, it's full! Nothing more will go in!
Nan-in puts the pot down. That's you, he says, more or less: like this cup, full of your own opinions. How can I show you anything until you empty it first?
That's the whole story: a teapot, a cup, and a puddle on the floor. A word about where it comes from.

teach.h: A TEACHING STORY, HARD TO TRACE.
teach.b: It reached English readers through a twentieth-century collection of Zen stories, and its earlier history in Japan is hard to trace, so hold it as a teaching story, not a court record.

teach.h: YOU CAN'T LEARN WHAT YOU KNOW.
teach.b: What it teaches is simple and hard: you can't learn what you think you already know. The professor didn't come to learn. He came to be confirmed.
Anything new Nan-in might have said would have spilled off the top of what was already there.
Zen has a word for the opposite state: shoshin, beginner's mind.
The Japanese teacher Shunryu Suzuki, who taught in America, built his talks around it, teaching that a beginner sees many possibilities where an expert sees few.
Emptying the cup doesn't mean throwing away everything you know.
It means leaving room: room for the other person to surprise you, room for a subject you think you've mastered to still have something to say. The cup is only useful for the space inside it.

how: Some Zen teachers start new students with beginner's mind, shoshin, and the cup of tea story is told in Zen centers and beyond them to describe coming to practice without assuming you already understand.

o: a master's calm, emptied of all thought
beginner's mind, open and ready to learn
the Zen tea ceremony's first pour

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: the story's history is well documented in old Japanese records
it reached English readers through a twentieth-century collection; its earlier history is hard to trace.
emptying the cup means throwing away everything you know
it means leaving room, so something new can still go in.
the professor came mostly to talk
he had read the books and had theories, and he talked while Nan-in made tea.

games.q: you're Nan-in. a visitor who says he wants to learn has talked for an hour. you've made tea. what do you do?
o: pour his cup until it overflows.
politely wait for him to finish.
games.why: he keeps pouring until the tea spills. when the visitor cries that it's full, Nan-in says: so are you. empty your cup first.

practice: If you have a cup and some water nearby, pour slowly, or just picture it, and stop at the moment just before full, when there's still a little room. Sit with that cup in front of you, and breathe.
Think of one subject, or one person, you're sure you already understand, and leave a little room at the top.

wordCard.voice: shoshin, beginner's mind. Nan-in poured tea until it spilled, to show a visitor he was too full of his own opinions to learn.

orig.note: Japanese, shoshin: beginner's mind, a Zen word for coming to anything fresh.

carryVoice: Your line: empty the cup. A full cup has no room for tea. Day forty-three.
